title: On-Metal NFC Labels vs Standard NFC Stickers
summary: Choose on-metal NFC labels ($0.20-$1.50) for metal surfaces and standard NFC stickers ($0.05-$0.30) for cardboard, plastic and glass. A standard sticker on solid metal reads at 0-5 mm or not at all; the on-metal ferrite layer restores 1-3 cm read range. Audit the surface first — the wrong label on metal is the most common NFC pilot failure. This comparison covers the physics, surface types, costs and a testing protocol.
heroPoints: Standard NFC stickers: $0.05-$0.30 per label, work reliably on cardboard, plastic, glass, paper and most non-conductive surfaces. Read range 2-4 cm on modern smartphones.

On-metal NFC labels. $0.20-$1.50 per label, include a ferrite absorber layer that restores 1-3 cm read range on solid metal surfaces. Mandatory for metal machinery, metal packaging, metal asset plates and metal rack labels.

Surface audit first: confirm whether the application surface is metal, metalized, near metal or non-metal before ordering samples. Wrong label on metal surface is the single most common NFC pilot failure.

sections.title: The physics — why metal breaks standard NFC labels
bullets: NFC operates at 13.56 MHz via magnetic inductive coupling. The reader's coil generates an alternating magnetic field, the label's antenna coil receives it, the tag chip harvests energy and modulates the response. Everything depends on the tag antenna being free to resonate at 13.56 MHz.

Conductive metal immediately adjacent to the tag antenna absorbs and dissipates magnetic field energy through eddy currents, detuning the antenna's resonant frequency and drastically reducing the signal received by the chip. The tag effectively 'shorts out' against the metal.

Detuning severity depends on metal type, metal thickness and air gap. Solid steel at zero gap is worst case. Standard NFC label reads at 0-5 mm or not at all. Thin foil at 1-2 mm air gap may read with reduced range. A 3-5 mm plastic spacer between the label and the metal often restores usable performance.

On-metal NFC labels add a layer of ferrite absorber (typically 0.1-0.3 mm thick) between the tag antenna and the adhesive backing. The ferrite redirects magnetic flux around the metal substrate rather than letting it induce eddy currents, preserving the antenna's resonance.
Good on-metal labels restore 60-80% of free-air read range. A standard NFC sticker reading at 4 cm on cardboard typically reads at 1-3 cm when converted to on-metal construction.

The ferrite layer adds cost ($0.10-$0.50 per label), weight (minimal) and thickness (0.5-1 mm total versus 0.2 mm for a standard sticker). These are all acceptable trade-offs when the alternative is a non-functional label.

sections.title: Surface types and how they behave
bullets: Solid metal (steel, aluminum, brass). Requires on-metal NFC label. This is the canonical case: equipment nameplates, industrial asset tags, metal furniture, metal tool handles, metal returnable containers.

Metalized plastic or metalized film. Behaves like metal for NFC purposes. Food packaging with aluminum foil liners, mylar-lined pharmaceutical blister packs and metalized shipping labels all require on-metal construction.

Metal with a plastic coating (painted, powder-coated, laminated). The coating thickness determines behavior. Thin paint layers (< 0.5 mm) do not decouple; use on-metal. Thicker coatings (2-5 mm) may provide enough air gap for a standard label to work, but test with representative samples.
Glass, ceramic, stone: non-conductive and NFC-transparent. Standard stickers work with full read range. No on-metal needed.
Wood, cardboard, paper: non-conductive. Standard stickers work well. Moisture can affect adhesion and slightly reduce read range but does not require on-metal construction.

Near-metal installations: a sticker applied to a plastic housing 10-20 mm from a metal chassis will read reliably in most cases but may show reduced range. Test with samples if the application is safety-critical.
Carbon fiber and conductive composites. Behave similarly to metal for NFC purposes. Use on-metal labels on carbon fiber drone frames, composite sports equipment and conductive polymer enclosures.

sections.title: Form factors and construction options
bullets: Thin on-metal labels — 0.5-0.8 mm total thickness, designed for applications where label profile matters (equipment nameplates, inside electronics enclosures, appliance control panels).
Thick on-metal labels — 1.5-3 mm with protective overlay, designed for industrial asset plates and outdoor applications where scratch and weather resistance matter.
Rigid on-metal tags. Rigid ABS, polycarbonate or PPS housings with the NFC inlay and ferrite laminated inside. Survive 5-10 years of industrial use, cost $1-$8 each depending on chip and housing.

Anti-metal tags: often used interchangeably with on-metal labels but typically refers to the rigid tag format. Proud Tek's RFID anti-metal tag product line covers UHF and HF variants for different application distances.

Screw-mounted versus adhesive-mounted. Industrial applications often require mechanical fastening. On-metal tags with screw holes survive vibration, abrasion and extreme temperature where adhesive labels fail.

Custom die-cut shapes. On-metal labels can be custom die-cut (circles, ovals, asymmetric shapes) but the ferrite layer adds production complexity. Allow 3-6 weeks lead time for custom shapes at first order.

Tamper-evident on-metal. Combining frangible substrate (fractures on removal attempt) with on-metal construction is possible but specialized. Specify tamper requirements upfront; retrofitting is rarely practical.

sections.title: Cost, volume and economics
bullets: Standard NFC sticker pricing. $0.05-$0.15 at 10,000+ volume, $0.10-$0.30 at 1,000-5,000 volume, $0.30-$0.80 at 100 or fewer.
On-metal NFC label pricing. $0.20-$0.40 at 10,000+ volume, $0.40-$0.80 at 1,000-5,000 volume, $0.80-$2.00 at 100 or fewer. The ferrite layer is the incremental cost driver.
Rigid on-metal tag pricing. $1-$8 each depending on housing material, chip and size. Typically sold in smaller volumes (100-5,000 per order) because they are used for higher-value assets.

ROI math: the question is not 'can we save 30 cents per label by using standard' but 'what is the cost of a non-functional label in our deployment'. A failed asset-tracking pilot with 500 mis-specified labels costs 100-500x the label savings.
Mixed deployments: many operations use both: on-metal labels for the 20% of applications with metal surfaces, standard stickers for the 80% on non-metal surfaces. Plan ordering by surface type.

Printing and personalization: both label types support thermal transfer printing of serial numbers, barcodes and text. On-metal labels with serialized QR codes and RFID identifiers are standard for industrial asset management.
Minimum order quantities: standard stickers MOQ 500-1,000, on-metal labels MOQ 500-1,000 for stock designs, 2,500-5,000 for custom designs. Budget lead time accordingly.

sections.title: Common deployment scenarios
bullets: Industrial asset tracking: machinery, tools, pallets, fixtures and returnable totes. On-metal labels or rigid anti-metal tags are the norm. Integrate with CMMS (computerized maintenance management systems) for inspection scheduling and work-order linkage.

IT asset management: laptops, servers, monitors, network equipment. Most modern laptops have plastic chassis and accept standard stickers; rack-mounted server hardware is metal and requires on-metal labels.
Fleet and vehicle tagging. Cars, trucks, trailers, intermodal containers. Rigid on-metal tags with screw or weld mounting, specified for outdoor UV, temperature and vibration.

Retail anti-theft and authentication. Luxury handbags and accessories with metal hardware require on-metal NFC tags for authentication taps to read reliably. Place tags in pockets, linings or inside hardware cavities.

Pharmaceutical and cosmetics packaging. Foil-lined blister packs and tubes require on-metal labels. Many brands embed the tag inside the outer carton rather than on the primary container for easier integration.

Smart building and facilities. Fire extinguishers (metal), HVAC equipment (metal), conference room signs (often metal), visitor badge holders (plastic). Specify on-metal for fire/HVAC/building-asset applications; plastic label holders are fine with standard stickers.
Event and hospitality: metal room signage, metal artwork frames, metal food-service equipment all benefit from on-metal tags for interactive guest experiences (tap for description, tap for reorder).

sections.title: Testing protocol and common mistakes
bullets: Surface audit first: photograph representative application surfaces, measure thickness of any non-metal coating, identify backing materials and mounting geometry. Share photographs with the label manufacturer before the RFQ.
Prototype order: order 10-25 samples of each candidate label construction. Apply to representative surfaces in realistic mounting positions. Test with the smartphone mix your users will have.

Field testing: read range under actual lighting, angles and user postures matters more than bench-top performance. A label that reads at 3 cm on a workbench but 5 mm when mounted 8 feet up on a piece of equipment fails in deployment.
Mistake 1 — ordering large volume before prototyping. A 5,000-label order of mis-specified stickers cannot be recovered; the tags are now committed scrap or return-to-vendor with restocking fees.
Mistake 2 — assuming painted metal works like plastic. Paint layers under 1 mm thick do not provide enough decoupling; use on-metal.
Mistake 3 — using on-metal labels where they aren't needed. On-metal construction costs 2-4x more than standard stickers with no benefit on non-metal surfaces. Don't overspend.

Mistake 4 — not accounting for label orientation. NFC read performance depends on the tag antenna orientation relative to the reader antenna. Specify preferred reader approach direction when mounting.

Mistake 5 — ignoring adhesive selection. Industrial surfaces often need high-strength acrylic or rubber-modified adhesives, not standard paper-sticker glue. Specify adhesive grade based on surface energy, temperature and outdoor exposure.

sections.title: Chip selection for on-metal and standard labels
bullets: {chip:nxp-ntag-213:short_name} — the value workhorse. {chip:nxp-ntag-213:user_bytes} bytes user memory, NDEF URL encoding, $0.05-$0.15 per chip. Fine for most brand-interaction and marketing use cases. Available in both standard and on-metal constructions.

{chip:nxp-ntag-215:short_name} — {chip:nxp-ntag-215:user_bytes} bytes user memory, useful for longer NDEF records (vCards, multi-URL, encoded analytics). Moderate cost increase over {chip:nxp-ntag-213:short_name}.

{chip:nxp-ntag-216:short_name} — {chip:nxp-ntag-216:user_bytes} bytes user memory, used when you need to store more data on-tag (not typical for simple URL redirects but common for offline-readable records).

{chip:nxp-ntag-424-dna:short_name} — cryptographic authentication with per-tap signed messages. The right choice when the tagged asset is high-value and counterfeiting risk is real (luxury goods, pharmaceuticals). Premium price but still works in both standard and on-metal formats.

UHF RFID alternatives: for longer-range applications (1-15 m) instead of NFC tap, UHF RAIN RFID on-metal tags are available. Different chip families (Monza R6, Impinj M700 series, Alien Higgs 9) and different reader infrastructure.

Chip versus antenna separation. The chip choice is independent of whether the label is on-metal construction. The same NTAG 213 chip can go into a standard sticker or an on-metal label; the antenna and ferrite differ, the chip stays the same.

faq.question: Can a standard NFC sticker be tested on metal anyway?
faq.answer: You can test it, but the result is usually a wasted order. Standard NFC stickers on solid metal read at 0-5 mm in best-case scenarios and often not at all. If your deployment is clearly on metal surfaces (equipment nameplates, metal packaging, metal asset plates), order on-metal samples directly. If the surface is ambiguous (painted metal, plastic-over-metal, near-metal plastic housings), order a small mixed sample pack of both constructions and test in the actual installation geometry. Don't commit large volumes until testing confirms which label construction works.

faq.question: Does on-metal always mean a harder, thicker label?
faq.answer: Thicker yes, harder not necessarily. On-metal labels add a 0.1-0.3 mm ferrite absorber layer between the antenna and the metal substrate, making total label thickness 0.5-1 mm compared to 0.2 mm for standard stickers. The label itself can still be a flexible film-based construction. The ferrite layer adds thickness but not rigidity. If your application needs a rigid tag (outdoor asset plates, screw-mounted equipment tags), specify rigid anti-metal tag construction rather than a flexible on-metal label.

faq.question: Will an on-metal label read on a non-metal surface?
faq.answer: Yes, but with reduced efficiency. On-metal labels are engineered assuming a metal substrate nearby; used on non-metal surfaces, they read at slightly reduced range compared to a standard sticker optimized for that surface. Practically the penalty is small — 2-3 cm on plastic instead of 3-4 cm. If you have mixed surfaces and want label-inventory simplicity, on-metal labels work universally at slightly higher cost and slightly reduced non-metal range. If you are optimizing both cost and performance, order both label types for their respective surface applications.

faq.question: What's the difference between on-metal labels and UHF anti-metal tags?
faq.answer: Frequency and application distance. On-metal NFC labels operate at 13.56 MHz for tap interactions at 0-3 cm — brand authentication, consumer engagement, local data exchange. UHF anti-metal tags operate at 860-960 MHz for bulk reader interrogation at 1-10 m — asset tracking, inventory counting, dock-door portal reads. Both solve the same metal-detuning physics but for different use cases. Many industrial asset-tracking deployments use UHF anti-metal rigid tags for warehouse visibility plus NFC tap interactions for local work-order completion on the same asset.

faq.question: How do I test NFC read performance on my specific metal surface?
faq.answer: Order 10 on-metal label samples and 5 standard sticker samples. Apply each to representative surfaces in realistic mounting positions. Test with the specific smartphone models your field users have (iPhone 13+, Samsung Galaxy S22+, Google Pixel 7+ are common reference devices; older or budget devices may have lower NFC power). Record read-range at various angles and operator approach directions. If read range is consistent at 1-2 cm across users and phones, the label is production-ready. If read range varies wildly (some users get 3 cm, others 0 mm), work with the manufacturer on antenna or ferrite optimization before scaling.

faq.question: Can I laminate or cover an on-metal label for outdoor durability?
faq.answer: Yes. Most on-metal labels support protective overlays (polyester, polycarbonate, PET film) laminated during manufacture for UV, abrasion and chemical resistance. The overlay adds 0.1-0.3 mm thickness and minimal read-range penalty. For harsh outdoor environments (direct UV sun, industrial chemical exposure, saltwater), specify outdoor-rated overlay during the RFQ. Avoid aftermarket adhesive film. Field-applied overlays trap air bubbles, shift adhesion and compromise long-term durability versus factory lamination.

faq.question: Do metal stickers work inside industrial asset tracking software like SAP EAM or IBM Maximo?
faq.answer: Yes. The label type is hardware; the data integration is software. Both NFC and UHF RFID labels can be serialized to link to CMMS/EAM asset records, work orders and inspection histories. Use the tag's serialized identifier (UID plus encoded asset ID) as the key into the asset management system. Most enterprise EAM platforms have RFID/NFC integration modules or support API-based record lookup from scan-generated events. The on-metal specification is purely a physical-layer decision; it doesn't change how the asset record flows through your software stack.
